reasoning: malyaan means full or filled, of a container, a bus or a page. For 'fed up' a Ramallah speaker says zah'aan or mish Taay'; for full after eating, shab3aan.
Shadda on ب and a long aa: kibbaaye, taa marbuta after ي being e. The ordinary Ramallah word for a drinking glass.
ظ is written TH per the scheme; in this learned word Ramallah speakers realise it as an emphatic z rather than an interdental. The feminine ending is -iyye.
ث is t, so مثلجة is respelled مْتَلّجِة, a Form II feminine participle shaped like m3allme. It describes icy, snow-covered weather; for snow actually falling a Ramallah speaker says 3am bitthallij.
The MSA diphthong aw becomes oo in Ramallah, and the medial hamza is written ': too'am, plural twaa'im.
il- assimilates to the sun letter ت. mish is the Palestinian negator before an adjective, and shaghghaale 'working' has shadda on غ with taa marbuta as e after ل.
ق glottalises even in this semi-legal word: 3a'aar, plural 3a'aaraat. Note the homograph عقار also means a drug or medication in formal Arabic, but the property sense is what is meant in Ramallah.
Emphatic ص as S, ح as 7, taa marbuta after ف as e. Means journalism as a profession as well as the press.
Word-initial hamza is written as the vowel a, then a y glide and long uu. The Levantine month name used in Ramallah, not sibtambar.
Medial hamza in ra'iis is written '; the final hamza of وزراء is not pronounced in speech, so I respell it وُزَرَا. Usually heard with the article as ra'iis il-wuzara.
ح is 7 and the vowel is ee, not ii: 7eefa.
The counted plural of alf in Palestinian is taalaaf, with the linking t, as in tlat taalaaf and arba3 taalaaf. The numeral loses its ending before it: 3ashr taalaaf.
English loan with long oo then aa: moobaayil. Equally common in Ramallah is jawwaal, which is the distinctly Palestinian word for a mobile phone.
Plural imperative of ittaSal is ittiSlu, shadda doubling ت. ع plus the article contracts to 3al-, and the hamza is written after that prefix, as in il-'usbuu3.
ع is 3 and the shadda on و doubles it: 3aduww. Plural a3daa'.
ث becomes t in Ramallah and ق is a glottal stop, so ثقة is respelled تِقَة, with taa marbuta as a after ق. Common in 3indo ti'a b nafso, 'he is self-confident'.
Long ii then the dual ending -een: miiteen. The Palestinian form of 200, from miyye.
b-imperfect first person of ba3at: bab3at, plus -lak 'to you (m.)'. masij is the English loan 'message', used for an SMS or chat message.
Word-initial hamza is written as the vowel; ق glottalises in conversation, in'ilaab, though news readers keep q. Means a coup d'etat.
Palestinian drops the first short vowel in the CiCaaC shape, as in ktaab and 7maar, giving slaa7. Plural islii7a.
Formal written Arabic; nobody says it in Ramallah conversation, where 'now' is halla'. The hamza is written after the article prefix, as in il-'usbuu3.
Imperative of 'aSS with the -li suffix: 'uSSli, emphatic ص doubled whole. shwayy 'a bit' has a doubled final y; ج is a moon letter so the article stays il-.
English 'user' borrowed with long uu. Literally the user, but in Ramallah speech shu il-yuuzir means 'what is the username', so the gloss holds.
The vowel is ee, not ii: ya reet. Everyday Ramallah way of saying 'I wish / if only', also used alone as a wistful yes.
ظ of نظيف surfaces as emphatic ض in Palestinian, and the first short vowel drops: nDiif. The spelling given already matches what is said.
